newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says Rwanda's army killed nearly 140 villagers.
newsitem.headline: UN says Rwanda's army killed nearly 140 villagers.

text.p: Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated troops have killed at least 137 villagers in the troubled northwest in an apparent reprisal for the murder of a government official and two other people, the U.N. human rights office said on Thursday.
Soldiers tied their victims in pairs with their shirt tails, made them lie face down and shot them in the head, it quoted a survivor as saying.
"Many civilians were summarily executed during the cordon-and-search operation," it said in a statement.

Dozens of bodies were found in banana plantations and in a eucalyptus forest following the army cordon-and-search operation in Ruhengeri on March 3, a day after unidentified men killed three people, including a tax collector, the statement said.

The statement did not give the ethnicity of the victims, but Ruhengeri, near Zaire's border, is populated mainly by the majority Hutu tribe and is the scene of an insurgency by Hutu rebels who played a key role in 1994's slaughter of Tutsis.
Villagers were gathered in a football stadium before the search, ordered to dig holes in the ground and then told to go look for the corpses of their family members and relatives.
Most corpses had fractured skulls and bullet wounds. Those who did not die immediately were beaten to death with clubs, witnesses told U.N. human rights observers.
Civilian authorities reported 157 killed but witnesses put the death toll much higher following the army search for the rebels, the statement said.
Rwandan military told U.N. rights officials that Ruhengeri's battalion commander was to blame for the killings, saying he "acted of his own accord", and that he had been arrested.

The London-based human rights group Amnesty International has reported hundreds of people killed in the tiny central African country this year and an increase in unlawful executions by army soldiers, many of whom are genocide survivors.

Since the killing of five U.N. human rights workers in the southwest in February, movements of U.N. staff and aid workers have been restricted, preventing them from investigating and reporting abuses and violence in the countryside.
